title: How strangers share secrets online

steps.p: Public-key cryptography gives each party a public key, shared freely, and a private key, kept secret.

steps.h: Lock with public, unlock with private
steps.p: Anything locked with your public key can only be unlocked with your private key — like an open padlock anyone can snap shut.
Your browser uses this to agree on a shared secret with a website, then switches to fast symmetric encryption for the conversation.

aside: This is what happens behind the padlock icon every time you visit an HTTPS site.

q: What does the padlock icon on an HTTPS website actually guarantee?
options: The site is trustworthy and safe
Your connection to that domain is encrypted and the domain's certificate checked out
why: Encryption to that domain — nothing more. Phishing sites get certificates easily too. The padlock means no one in between can read your traffic, not that the site is honest.

statement: Incognito or private browsing hides your browsing from your internet provider and employer.
why: False. It only stops your browser from saving history and cookies on your device. Your network, internet provider and the sites you visit can still see your traffic.

q: Why does a phone charge quickly to about 80% and then slow down?
options: Lithium-ion batteries switch to constant-voltage charging near full to avoid damage
The last 20% is a bigger capacity
why: Battery protection. Charging switches from constant current to constant voltage, with current tapering off near full. Pushing hard at high charge would stress and age the cells.

title: A QR code can still scan with up to 30% of it damaged or covered.
detail: QR codes include Reed–Solomon error correction, the same family of math used on CDs. The highest level adds enough redundancy to rebuild about 30% of the data — which is why logos can sit in the middle.

q: How does a microwave oven heat food?
options: Microwaves make water molecules rotate back and forth, and the motion becomes heat
why: Spinning water molecules. Water molecules have positive and negative ends that try to line up with the oscillating field, about 2.45 billion times a second, and friction turns that into heat.

statement: Microwave ovens cook food from the inside out.
why: False. Microwaves penetrate only a few centimeters. The outer layers heat directly, and the center warms mostly by conduction — which is why thick food stays cold in the middle.

q: How does a phone's touchscreen detect your finger?
options: Your finger changes the electric field in a grid of electrodes, altering capacitance
why: Capacitance. Your body conducts electricity, so touching the glass disturbs the electric field at that point. It is why a normal glove doesn't work.

title: How sites should store your password

steps.p: A well-built site stores a hash: a one-way scramble that cannot be reversed back into the password.
A random value is mixed in for each user, so two identical passwords produce different hashes, and precomputed tables are useless.
Algorithms like bcrypt or Argon2 are deliberately slow, making billions of guesses expensive for an attacker.

aside: If a site can email you your old password, it is storing it wrongly.

q: Why is an authenticator app safer than SMS codes for two-factor login?
options: SMS can be intercepted, notably by SIM-swap fraud
why: SIM swapping. Attackers trick a phone carrier into moving your number to their SIM, receiving your codes. App codes are generated on your own device.

title: One of the first recorded computer "bugs" was a real moth.
detail: In 1947, engineers found a moth stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II and taped it into the logbook, noting the "first actual case of bug being found". The term was already engineering slang.

q: About how many unique IPv4 internet addresses are possible?
why: About 4.3 billion (2³²). That ran out as the internet grew, which is why home networks share one public address and why IPv6, with 2¹²⁸ addresses, was created.

statement: Deleting a file and emptying the trash usually erases its data immediately.
why: False. Typically the system just marks the space as free, and the data stays until overwritten. That is why recovery tools work — and why secure erasure exists.

options: Translates names like example.com into numeric IP addresses
why: The internet's phone book. Computers route by IP address; DNS lets people use memorable names. When DNS fails, sites seem down even though they're running.

title: About 99% of data crossing between continents travels through undersea cables, not satellites.
detail: Hundreds of fiber-optic cables, many only the width of a garden hose, run across ocean floors. Ship anchors and fishing gear are their most common threats.

q: Why does an e-reader's e-ink screen use almost no power while showing a page?
options: Its charged ink particles stay in place without power, so energy is only used to change the page
why: It's bistable. Black and white particles are moved by an electric field and then stay put. Phone screens must refresh constantly, which is why e-readers last weeks.

statement: Your phone battery lasts longer if you always drain it to 0% before recharging.
why: False. That was true for old nickel batteries. Lithium-ion batteries age faster with deep discharges; keeping them roughly between 20% and 80% is gentler.

q: Besides navigation, what critical service relies heavily on GPS satellites?
options: Precise timing for phone networks, power grids and financial systems
why: Timekeeping. GPS satellites carry atomic clocks, and countless systems synchronize to them. A GPS outage would disrupt far more than maps.

title: Let a password manager remember for you
body: Reusing passwords means one leaked site unlocks the rest. A password manager makes a unique strong password for every site and fills it in for you.
challenge: Change the password on your most important account (usually email) to a unique one today.

statement: 5 GHz Wi-Fi is faster than 2.4 GHz, but passes through walls less well.
why: True. Higher frequencies carry more data but are absorbed more by walls and floors. That trade-off is why routers offer both bands.
